title: Penn State alum Amelia White ties NWSL record for fastest goal
author: Noah Radio | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State women’s soccer alum Amelia White tied the NWSL’s fastest goal record when she scored 22 seconds into the Kansas City Current match on Friday night.

White spent four years in Happy Valley, appearing in 88 total games. In 2025, she closed her Penn State career by starting all 21 games, scoring 6 goals and earning second team All-Big Ten honors.

White now shares the record with KC Current teammate Michelle Cooper, who set the mark in June 2023.

The Current are back in action on Aug. 22, taking on Seattle Reign FC.

title: Former Penn State QB Drew Allar shines in Pittsburgh Steelers preseason debut
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Drew Allar’s first game in a Pittsburgh Steelers uniform couldn’t have gone much better.

Allar played a majority of the second half, going 10-for-13 for 153 yards and three total touchdowns and leading the Steelers to a 28-9 victory over the Green Bay Packers.

The former Nittany Lion began his night with just over four minutes left in the third quarter and played the rest of the second half.

After multiple handoffs, Allar found former Iowa wide receiver Kaden Wetjen on a slant for his first completion as an NFL quarterback, leading Wetjen to take it 74 yards down to the one yard line.

Two plays later, Allar kept the ball and ran it into the end zone on a read option, scoring his first professional touchdown.

Allar’s next drive was his most impressive. He led the Steelers down the field, making quick reads and firing strikes to a plethora of receivers. His two longer completions to Max Hurleman for 18 and 21 yards, respectively, were the best of the drive, hitting him in stride with each pass.

Allar’s composure in the pocket and quick decision making was tested in the red zone, where he stepped back out of the collapsing pocket and tried to hit a receiver, ultimately leading to a pass interference. The footwork continues to be an area of work for Allar, as it’s been a focal point dating back to rookie minicamp.

The drive was capped off with a 5-yard touchdown pass to Wetjen, with Allar adding his second touchdown in as many drives.

The third and final possession of Allar’s first game continued to show his decisiveness. Two pass interference calls continued the drive, and Allar took advantage. He finished his impressive debut with a four-yard pass in the flat to former Indiana tight end Riley Nowakowski, going a perfect three-for-three in drives ending in touchdowns.

Allar remains in a quarterback battle with second-year pro Will Howard for the 2026 backup role, but also for a potential spot as the Steelers’ future quarterback. Howard finished the game 7-for-9 for 86 yards, leading a two-minute drive for a touchdown to end the first half.

title: ‘It's more strategic’ | Schematics, execution key for Penn State’s new practice philosophy
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
This offseason, Terry Smith paid a visit to the Pittsburgh Steelers and spectated one of their training camp sessions, taking notes on what he could replicate to make Penn State’s practices similar to those at the professional level.

One of the many changes to the program since the arrival of Matt Campbell, the practice philosophy features more emphasis on the schematic approach and how players execute their roles on the field.

“We're probably more geared to how the NFL does it,” Smith said on Thursday. “It's more strategic. There's certain days that we're going to do a little bit more contact, whereas in the past we did contact almost every day.”

In concept, for the majority of practices, the defense would run a “tag-off mode” when approaching the ball carrier from the side. When the contact is head-on, however, the players have been allowed to make a brief impact to bring intensity.

Additionally, Smith confirmed that all reps have been executed at full speed, just without too much contact, lowering the risk of potential injuries from heavy tackling. The new structure also hasn’t taken away the toughness factor that Campbell has preached.

“It's a fine line, and our camp here has been really demanding,” Smith said. “I do think we have a tough football team, and that starts with the head coach. He's tough. He's tough on us, he's tough on the team.”

The point of the new practice philosophy is for the coaching staff to evaluate the team’s playmaking abilities in a controlled environment, and it’s become more about who can execute consistently on the concepts the coaching staff has been teaching.

Specifically, the coaches have been looking into whether each player knows their assignment, can read the opposing scheme and put thought into action when the ball is snapped. Physicality is an additional element thrown into the mix when appropriate.

Wide receivers coach Kashif Moore noted that the players who aren’t on the field are gaining experience through “mental reps.”

“It's not a new install, so kids should be able to retain what we're trying to get done,” safeties coach Deon Broomfield said. “You're trying to make it as game-like as possible, and see who can actually execute at a high level.”

Campbell said on Thursday that the Nittany Lions have had two of their heaviest practices in the past two days, allowing for the coaching staff to “evaluate fundamentally.”

However, the true test of this will be the upcoming scrimmage game at Beaver Stadium on Saturday, where the team will be given the green light to play at full throttle.

“The offense is drawing up a play to defeat the defense, we're drawing up a play to defeat the offense,” Smith said. “Where are the advantages and disadvantages? And as they show up full speed, then when you chime in with the full speed, like contact on Saturday, you'll see really well.”

title: Penn State players, coaches ‘excited’ for Saturday scrimmage in Beaver Stadium
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s first game in Beaver Stadium in 2026 is a little under a month away, and for a lot of players, it’ll be the first time playing in front of the Nittany Lion faithful.

In anticipation of that, the team will put the pads on for a scrimmage in Beaver Stadium on Saturday, marking the closest thing to real-game plays this fall.

“I just think getting in the stadium, forcing ourselves to play in that stadium, so many guys that are new, and obviously getting in there as much as we possibly can before the start of the season, I think is really important for us,” Matt Campbell said during his media availability Thursday.

The biggest importance of scrimmaging in Beaver Stadium on Saturday is the fact it’s a full go for everyone available. Taking on live hits in a scrimmage can better acclimate the team for in-game hits during the regular season.

During this tune-up, the coaches and team are looking at it as a game in order to simulate what things will look like when Marshall heads to Happy Valley on Sept. 5.

“It's just like a game approach,” safeties coach Deon Broomfield said. “So you're looking for execution, alignments, assignments, reads and keys. Can guys do the things that we've been emphasizing the last couple days?”

Practice gets reps in for the players, but it also sometimes shows how the players will do against competition. Nothing matches up to putting the pads on and going through a full scrimmage at Beaver Stadium, however.

Wide receivers coach Kashif Moore hopes to see “consistency” and “physicality” on Saturday as it’s “the closest thing to a game” the team will have before the first week of the 2026 campaign.

For the players, the excitement level is building. While Saturday will be able to fulfill some of that anticipation new players have, it won’t match up to what they’ll see in three weeks.

“We drive past it every day, going to the hotel every night, and it’s lit up outside,” wide receiver Chase Sowell said. “I literally look and drive right past it, and I’m just like, ‘I can’t even imagine how the thing’s gonna be rocking,' September 5th and the days to come, but it’s always been my dream.”

Penn State recently announced that the home opener will be the annual Stripe Out, which will likely bring a louder environment than a typical nonconference home game. The Stripe Out will also ring in the Campbell era with a welcome from one of the loudest environments in the entire country.

“I never thought I’d be playing at this level or at a university like this, so I don’t take any of it for granted, and I definitely won’t take any of the people that come to support us for granted,” Sowell said. “I’m definitely excited for sure.”

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell discusses fall camp, position change
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Fall camp is just about halfway over for Penn State, with less than a month remaining until opening kickoff.

Matt Campbell took the podium in the Lasch Building after the second padded practice to discuss player health, the pressure that comes with being a head coach and a position change.

Here’s a look at what Campbell said Thursday.

Player health

While Penn State has dealt with several long-term injuries in recent years before the season even began, Campbell delivered good news about his team on Thursday.

When asked specifically about how safety Jeremiah Cooper and linebacker Alex Tatsch are trending as they continue to rehab from long-term injuries, Campbell noted that no other players were dealing with significant injuries so far in fall camp.

“I think for sure by this part of camp, you’re going to have guys that are dinged up,” Campbell said. “The great win for us is there’s nobody that I would say at this time who we won't see in Game 1.”

One of the more notable minor injuries mentioned was defensive tackle Dallas Vakalahi. Campbell confirmed he picked up an injury early in camp, but isn’t expected to miss more than a week.

On the other hand, fellow defensive tackle Armstrong Nnodim is back to full strength after an injury that set him back at the start of camp.

“He finally looks healthy here the last couple of days,” Campbell said. “It’s going to be really fun to see what he continues to progress to.”

Earn it attitude

While it’s been less than nine months since Campbell took the helm at Penn State, he knows his position is fragile.

“In the world we live in, I think you’re always in a prove-it type situation,” Campbell said.

Throughout his coaching career, Campbell has climbed the ranks through programs without being fired. However, both he and the rest of the college football world have seen what can happen, including with former Penn State coach James Franklin, who was fired in October after taking the squad to the College Football Playoff semifinals the year prior.

With that pressure in mind, Campbell has built a staff he could depend on. He again mentioned the alignment of values throughout the coaching staff and the entirety of the football program, standing near the new culture wall with words like “legacy,” “faith” and “humility” on it.

“You hire a staff that you believe in and you know what they can get accomplished,” Campbell said. “That’s part of the journey.”

After 15 years as a head coach, Campbell is still in an earn-it situation. However, he’s thankful for the past and is excited for what’s to come.

“If it ended tomorrow, I’d be able to look in the mirror and be really proud of what we have all accomplished, no matter where we’ve been,” Campbell said.

Position change

Peyton Falzone arrived at Penn State in January as the top-rated quarterback from Pennsylvania in his class. Eight months later, his future at that position is up in the air.

As first reported by Sean Fitz of On3, Campbell confirmed on Thursday that Falzone is working on a switch from quarterback to tight end.

“What’s best for him and maybe best for the football team right now was his ability to see what he could do (at tight end),” Campbell said. “We’re really excited about what his future can entail.”

What began as full team reps at the beginning of camp to evaluate and see what different players were capable of turned into special play moments for Falzone. The quarterback-turned-tight end made several big catches during those early drills which led to the spot he’s in today.

Falzone has spent the last two days practicing at his new position and has already made a mark. But Campbell said “it’s not an easy move to make,” and there’s still a lot of practice to be done for Falzone.

“Peyton stood out,” Campbell said. “Peyton’s a guy who’s got so much athleticism. Is there more that we can do early on that can help our football team in some way?”

title: Column | Which Penn State teams will shine or slip in the fall?
author: Gavin Leonard | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State’s fall sports were a study of the extremes during the 2025-26 season. While some teams reached new heights, others finished the year searching for answers.

As the new season approaches, anticipation is building in Happy Valley. Yet, with expectations comes the possibility that some teams rise while others fall short.

Here’s how I think the Nittany Lions will pan out this fall.

Men’s Soccer - Competitive Season

When you hit rock bottom, the only way to go is up.

After a lackluster season where Penn State finished last in the Big Ten, they followed by losing midfielder Caden Grabfelder, a key contributor and veteran to the team, in the transfer portal.

Grabfelder’s absence left a leadership void, but new head coach Rob Dow didn’t arrive without filling the need.

With Dow’s championship pedigree, a revamped coaching staff, and incoming players who fit his style of play, the Nittany Lions could be more competitive in 2026.

Women’s Soccer - NCAA Tournament Appearance

Following a loss in the second round of the NCAA tournament to one-seeded Virginia, Coach Erica Dambach’s team is looking to return with a vengeance.

Replacing top goal scorer Kaitlyn MacBean’s offensive production will be a tough task. While Paige Kalal and Aubrey Kulpa are talented forwards who can lead the offense, it won’t be enough for Penn State to take a significant step forward.

Wrestling - National Championship Favorite

The reigning national champions continued their dynasty by dominating the 2025 season.

Individual national champions Mitchell Mesenbrink, Luke Lilledahl, and PJ Duke headline a loaded roster full of talent. Anything short of another NCAA title would be viewed as a disappointment.

Women’s Volleyball - Title Contender

Coming off a disappointing loss in the NCAA second round, the Nittany Lions still feature a significant amount of elite talent.

Kennedy Martin, Alexis Stuckey and Izzy Starck are all names that look poised to lead the team to similar success as last season.

Men’s Hockey - NCAA Tournament Appearance

Penn State Men’s hockey finished the season 21-14-2 with a second consecutive NCAA Tournament bid, but lost No. 1 overall pick Gavin McKenna to the 2026 NHL Draft.

Filling his absence will be a difficult challenge, but the Nittany Lions have the roster to do so. Led by Jackson Smith, a legitimate Hobey Baker candidate, Penn State is primed to finish top four in the Big Ten and return to the NCAA Tournament.

Women’s Ice Hockey - Conference Frontrunner

Penn State won both the AHA championship and national title last season, and look poised to be equally successful this year.

The team’s returning stars are more than capable of leading the Nittany Lions back to the top of their conference standings with a chance to win their fourth title in five years.

Men’s Basketball - Middle-of-the-Pack Finish

After losing 13 out of 15 conference games, Penn State lost nine scholarship players during the offseason.

In a highly competitive Big Ten, expectations for the Nittany Lions should remain minimal. At best, Penn State will finish in the middle of the Big Ten standings.

Women’s Basketball - Big Ten Climber

Tanisha Wright will enter her first year as head coach attempting to revitalize a team who went 6-12 in the Big Ten and lost their leading scorer Kiyomi McMiller in the transfer portal.

The Lady Lions will sport a newly-revamped roster this season, though, and could take steps to be more competitive in this season’s conference slate.

Field Hockey - Transition Period

New head coach Hannah Prince inherits a Penn State team coming off of a year that fell well below their standards. Bringing the team back to the top of the standings won't happen after one season, but we can expect clear signs of progress.

A roster that added nine newcomers, including former All-Big Ten Second Team selection Ella Gaitan, gives Penn State a legitimate chance to climb the standings after a disappointing 2025.

Football - Bowl Game Appearance

In comparison to the elite level of play that fans are used to watching, last season was about as disappointing as could be. The Nittany Lions began the 2025 season ranked second in the AP Preseason Top 25 and ended the season with a 7-6 record and a 22-10 win in the Pinstripe Bowl.

However, with a not-so competitive schedule, combined with the arrival of Rocco Becht and Benjamin Brahmer and the hiring of Matt Campbell, the Nittany Lions are due for a bounce back season.

title: Penn State wrestling commit Clinton Shepherd to forgo senior year, join Nittany Lions
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State has added more depth to its lineup.

2027 commit Clinton Shepherd will leave high school a year early and join Penn State ahead of the 2026-27 season.

Shepherd is coming off a state championship season in Indiana, going 38-1 at 150 pounds, with his only loss against now-Minnesota wrestler Tyler Dekraker.

Shepherd's addition to the team comes nine months after his commitment in December, which added to a loaded 2027 class. With his bump in year, he leaves Landon Sidun, Grey Burnett, Gavin Mangano, James Whitbred and Will Soto.

The decision from Shepherd and Penn State isn't uncommon. Last year, Oklahoma State's Jax Forrest joined the Cowboys midway through the year and ultimately competed for the team, winning a national title. But within the program, Levi Haines and Tyler Kasak both made similar moves to get into the wrestling room early and compete against national title contenders every day.

Shepherd's eligibility clock will begin this year, with five years ahead of him. He's expected to compete in college open tournaments throughout the year. He projects as a middleweight wrestler anywhere at 149, 157 or 165 during his collegiate career.

title: ‘Best running back room that I’ve had’ | Penn State RBs buying into depth of room
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s running back room could be as deep as it’s been in years, which is saying a lot given the past four years have featured Kaytron Allen and Nick Singleton, who both are now in the NFL.

But this season, the depth of the room will show out more than just the top guys.

“The one fortunate thing that I will say is this is the best running back room that I've had since I've been coaching in college, top to bottom, and I've been very fortunate to have that room,” running back coach Savon Huggins said at local media day on Friday.

The running back room, which features multiple players who could be the top running back, has bought into the depth of the room. They’re helping each other out rather than just strictly competing against each other.

Some of the running backs have strengths that are weaknesses for others in the room, and the way they help each other has been talked about for months, dating back to before the Blue-White Practice.

“Some guys right now today maybe, has better open field awareness than another person, but someone runs better between the tackles,” Huggins said. “But I think that's the challenge, is like, can everybody work on their particular gap, right? If they can all work on each other's gaps, I think that allows them to make my job harder and who I'm going to play.”

The strengths of each running back allows for the possibility of the group staying fresh instead of one bell cow running back who’s carrying the workload. That could have major benefits later in the season, with none of the four — Carson Hansen, James Peoples, Quinton Martin Jr. and Cam Wallace — having had major work during a single week.

The players understand that, and they know that all of them being better helps each other out. It’s the same mentality that Singleton and Allen had the past four years, recognizing that even though they’re not on the field as often, that’s actually making them better.

“We got a heck of a group man,” Wallace said. “This running back room, man, all of us can start a game off and play. It's just, we're just competitors in this group, just making each other better.”

The recognition of this stems from the veteran presence. Hansen’s entering his fourth year of college football while Peoples is entering his third. Both Martin and Wallace have both had playing time in years prior as well.

That leadership has Penn State’s room ready for the present and the future, with the older backs leading by example and helping the younger guys, including freshman D’Ante Sheffey.

“They may not say anything, but they're watching your mannerisms,” Huggins said. “They're watching your routine and your practice habits. They're watching how you conduct yourself in the weight room. They’re watching what time you show up to meetings.”

Huggins’ coaching has already revitalized the new-look running back room, which could be a committee of rushers rather than one or two lead backs.

“We all making each other better,” Wallace said. “We all correcting each other. We all taking full accountability of all each other’s faults and what we do right.”

Penn State linebacker Kooper Ebel was named to the Butkus Award watch list, given annually to the top linebacker in college football.

Ebel is slated to be the Nittany Lions' starting MIKE linebacker this year.

title: Off the record | Friend or foe
author: Miss Behave I The Daily Collegian
description:
Editor’s Note: Off the record is a weekly column written by a fourth-year Collegian staffer under an alias. It aims to promote a space for honest conversations about love, sex and relationships. Those interested in sharing their experiences or submitting a topic can do so through this anonymous form.

Dear reader,

A couple of weeks ago, I wrote a column about red flags I’ve encountered in past partners. From a whiny momma’s boy to being BFF’s with his exes, I shared many details on how my terrible taste in men can save you from future problems.

Clearly romantic relationships are riddled with red flags, but there are certain behaviors we should be avoiding when it comes to our friends as well. When it comes to our friends, there’s a specific kind of blindness we apply to their wrongdoings. We write it off as quirky flaws, tell ourselves, “They didn’t mean that in a bad way,” even when they probably did. Even when it’s behavior we wouldn’t tolerate in any other relationships.

After 21 years of life, I’ve become pretty good at spotting the biggest signs that trouble is ahead. Let me cue you in.

Body shaming

This is an absolute no-no. The minute a friend starts commenting on your body, eating habits, or size of your clothes, you need to start rethinking how important this person is to you.

If you’re already secure in your body image, that’s going to change real quick if this person sticks around. They’ll ruin shopping and going out to eat because nothing is more precious to them than their body. Because of that, you're inevitably forced to care about yours.

Gossiping being the only form of conversation

Listen, I’m not going to be a hypocrite and tell you that I don’t gossip. But I can still hold a conversation that doesn’t involve talking about someone else.

Some of my past friendships completely revolved around others' misfortune. It was the focus of every dinner and every hangout. Generally speaking, this means the relationship isn’t rooted in genuine connection. Therefore, it isn’t going to last.

But go ahead and think of it in a selfish way, too: If they’re talking so frequently about other people to you, they’re talking about you behind your back frequently too. End of story.

Forcing you out of your comfort zone

This is coming from someone whose anxiety and fears dominate their life. If your friends are forcing you to do things you aren’t comfortable doing, then they simply don’t respect you.

I despise roller coasters, so instead of pressuring me to ride with them, I’ve become the designated purse holder. I hate driving, so my beautiful, amazing friends often take me as their passenger. Making your friends feel safe and included is the bare minimum.

Thriving on male validation

I would never let a man dictate my every move, and I certainly wouldn’t tolerate my friends doing the same. This doesn’t mean having a boyfriend or friends who are men and listening to their opinions. I’m talking about letting a man tell them what to do and blindly following, just for the sake of earning their satisfaction.

Friends like this tend to talk about men all the time. I still talk to my friends about bad hookups, and I definitely talk to them about good hookups, but my talk of men is the same as my gossiping: brief, and not without me intellectualizing the new few sentences that come out of my mouth just to compensate for it occurring even briefly.

Also, beware of a friend who’s buddy-buddy with your ex. If they continuously listen to you talk about how someone hurt you and remain friends with them, sound the alarms.

Feeling the need to protect yourself around them

If you’re afraid to share information with them, you're subconsciously withholding for a reason. You recognize they aren’t worthy keepers of your deep, dark secrets. Or, the most basic, boring story about your professor you’ve told one thousand times over.

You know yourself best, so if you get that feeling that surface-level conversation is all they're going to get, then stick to your gut and avoid giving them any conversation at all.

Forever playing the victim

Nothing is ever their fault, and they're always ready to end things at the sight of conflict. If they’re constantly seeking pity and sympathy, but can’t return the favor, it’s a no from me. I want you to know that leaving a situation like this doesn’t make you a horrible person or undeserving of friends; you’ll know when enough is enough.

You deserve to be friends with people who can take accountability for their actions and are willing to see things through even when it gets tough.

Climbing the social ladder

A friend to all is a friend to none. You’ll encounter people who are using you to get their next big “thing,” and once they get it, they’re gone. Maybe it’s a cooler friend group or access to spaces that make them seem more important than they are. Whatever the case may be, real friends don’t step over you to get to a higher point in their lives.

If they’re ditching you last minute or waiting to confirm plans until they see who else is available, do yourself a favor and start distancing.

Minimizing your wins

If they continuously downplay your victories, they don’t care. It’s sad, but true. You’ve probably noticed that they can’t even be bothered to fake a smile until the conversation is over. Or maybe they do, but when you turn away, you can see the jealous glint in their eyes in your periphery. Maybe they start talking about how their latest victory awards them a much larger trophy.

Authentic friendship doesn’t rely on shrinking and belittling you to be successful. You should notice that even when you turn away, your real friends will still be smiling.

Navigating female friendships in your college years is difficult. There are a lot of moving parts, and a lot to learn. You’re a reflection of the company you keep, so be sure to surround yourself with friends who mirror the love and respect you have for yourself.

Until next time,

Miss Behave

title: During NSO, orientation leaders aim to provide a ‘safe space’ for incoming students
author: Carly Marnich | For The Collegian
description:
During the hot, sticky days of summer, State College lacks its usual whirr of cars, its expected flurry of students. That is, until New Student Orientation (NSO) kicks off, and a new group gets a taste of their very first year.

The mandatory two-day program, held on multiple dates throughout the late spring and early summer, helps students and their families become familiar with campus resources, schedule courses for their first semester and meet other students, faculty and staff.

Those that serve as mentors for incoming first-year students during the program, orientation leaders, are current undergraduate students themselves. They guide students through a variety of activities, including icebreakers and group dinners. But a big part of the program lies in these leaders sharing advice based on their own experiences.

For Ashna Thadathil, a fourth-year studying computer science, applying to be an orientation leader was a way to give back to the community she said gave her so much.

Thadathil didn’t experience new student orientation as a first-year, since she’s an international student, and she said her decision to become one stemmed from that experience. After connecting with a mentor through the international students webinar, she said she wanted to offer students the same support she received.

“I met so many beautiful people here, and each one of them taught me something,” Thadathil said.

Despite the long hours and tiring moments, she said her NSO experience was rewarding.

At the conclusion of the program, Thadathil said orientation leaders receive airmail feedback from students.

“There were students writing that I made them feel comfortable and was a safe space for them,” Thadathil said.

Lucy Hinkle, a third-year studying health policy and administration, said she had never had an extroverted personality until becoming an NSO leader.

Hinkle wasn’t actively searching for a job when she stumbled upon the application, and she said starting the job was a learning experience.

“Every time I would walk away from a program, I was always most rewarded by the questions section with the students,” Hinkle said.

Her favorite, she said, was being asked if students really carry umbrellas to class. Hinkle said she could get things off of her chest and add a personal touch when asked “silly” questions.

She said one of the hardest parts is meeting new students where they’re at. Though she said she prepares for weeks ahead of orientation’s beginning, when she’s face-to-face with students, it just comes down to committing to presenting.

“Everyone you’re working with is in this transitional period of life,” Hinkle said. “Although I’ve experienced that transition, it’s different to experience it for the first time.”

Trevor Rzasa, second-year studying psychology, was involved in student leadership as a marching band member in high school and wanted to carry that into his college experience, which is exactly how he wound up spending some summer days as an orientation leader.

He said the people are what made NSO so special for him, and that those on its directing team were welcoming and took the job seriously.

The students, too, Rzasa said, were a remarkable aspect of his experience.He said some of his favorite moments were when first-year students approached him one-on-one about concerns or excitement. He said he felt “honored” to help so many students by pulling from his own experiences.

With a younger brother who’s an incoming first-year at Penn State, Rzasa had the opportunity to relive the start of his own journey on campus. He said he now feels more connected to Penn State as a university and the community that makes it.

“Not every little detail from my own orientation stuck out in my head. By teaching students about Penn State’s value and history, I now know more about it,” Rzasa said.

title: With sustainability in mind, students thrift, repair their way into fall fashion
author: Allison Shanley | For The Collegian
description:
While shopping for new sneakers before long walks to class, or a new top before game days, some students have a priority to keep their fashion trendy.

For many, gone are the days of not having to worry about the cost of clothes. But by sifting through thrift racks in State College and doing at-home repairs, students can have a refreshed wardrobe without it costing a fortune, too.

As the store owner of Love It Upcycle Boutique on North Atherton Street, Deb Love knows the back-to-school shopping season well. Loves’ shelves are frequented by shoppers looking for more mature, luxury items, like purses and formal attire, but on a budget.

Love opened her first store in Huntingdon, Pennsylvania, a quaint borough about 50 minutes south of State College. Growing up, her family visited downtown State College for its thrifting selection. Her history in the area, she said, is what influenced her to open her second store in State College.

Many people come there to shop, and she said the community aspect of the store is what makes the boutique possible. But the store buys clothes off of people, too; a form of recycling, Love said.

“There's so many people that come in to sell us their clothes and they say, ‘We used to just throw our clothes away,’” Love said.

Love said she often collaborates with her neighbor-store, Plato's Closet, to swap pieces that fit each respective secondhand store's aesthetic.

While shopping secondhand helps students save money, it also lends to cutting down on the excess of fast fashion products.

Buying secondhand clothes helps decrease the 85% of clothing materials that wind up in landfills every year, according to research compiled by the Geneva Environment Network. Its research reports around 71% of clothing consumers have goals of adopting a more sustainable approach to fashion, but 62% still purchase fast fashion.

Leah Rau, a third-year studying secondary education, is a learning coordinator for the environmental science course Biological Science 3. Rau said the class gave her insight on tactics to shop sustainably and give pieces a longer lifespan.

“I would really advise people to know people that have similar interests,” Rau said. “Ask, ‘Does that person know how to sew?’ It's pretty awesome to indulge and share skills with each other.”

As a learning coordinator, Rau said that teaching practicality by utilizing her community has been the most effective way to promote acting with sustainability. Rau said she prioritizes shopping seasonally instead of annually to reduce waste, and she only shops for pieces she needs.

“It's mostly thrifting specific items I need,” Rau said. “I'll up-cycle my clothes mostly, right now I like taking off the collar of my shirt and making it off the shoulder. You can style T-shirts a thousand different ways.”

Upcycling pieces is an activity that focuses on the pieces already in your closet. It helps the environment to keep clothes hanging in the closet instead of laying in a dump, but it’s also a project to get your creative gears going.

Ash Knox, a second-year studying business management, said she creates things so she no longer has to buy them at the store.

“I started small 'cause I don't have anybody to teach me,” Knox said. “Teaching myself how to sew, I started making cosmetic and toiletry bags, making different patchworks and things like that.”

Knox began the practice of shopping sustainably in high school, influenced by her sister who she said frequently spoke of the unsafe working conditions in which many fast fashion items are produced. Earthday reports that this, alongside unfair wages, are common in the industry.

Additionally, factory workers are exposed to carbon emissions in all stages of fast fashion production, from material creation to construction of the piece, according to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. These emissions make up 10% of greenhouse gas emissions annually.

“Ultimately, fashion is something that's very important to people, " Knox said. “It is a part of your identity, and more people have the privilege to have access to clothing through secondhand shopping.”

title: Penn State men’s soccer schedule preview, what to expect in 2026
author: Noah Radio | For The Collegian
description:
Penn State men’s soccer is gearing up for a new era under Rob Dow, who was hired last December to replace Jeff Cook as the Nittany Lions’ head coach. He’s tasked with turning around a program that finished dead last in the Big Ten each of the past two seasons.

Dow comes from the University of Vermont, where he won the national championship in 2024. At the helm of the Catamounts, Dow earned a 129-41-21 record while taking the team to five straight NCAA Tournaments.

In 2025, the Nittany Lions won just one conference game and earned a 5-8-4 overall record.

Dow will make his regular season debut when Mercyhurst comes to town on Aug. 20. Penn State dominated the Lakers 5-0 last season and looks for more of the same here.

The team will then travel to Missouri State and attempt to avenge last year’s home loss before returning home for a three-game home stand against Pittsburgh, Bucknell and Yale.

When Pitt comes to town on Aug. 28, so will former Nittany Lion Caden Grabfelder. Grabfelder transferred down Route 22 this offseason after three standout seasons in Happy Valley. In his Penn State career, Grabfelder started 45 of 49 career games and was selected by CF Montréal with the No. 50 overall pick in the 2025 MLS SuperDraft.

After Grabfelder’s homecoming, the Nittany Lions will prepare for Big Ten play with Bucknell on Sept. 1, then Yale on Sept. 4. Last season, Bucknell finished 9-4-5 in the Patriot League, and Yale went just 3-9-3 in the Ivy.

On Sept. 11, the conference slate opens with a bang as the Nittany Lions travel to Seattle for a matchup with the defending national champions of Washington. The Huskies are ranked No. 1 in the United Soccer Coaches Preseason Poll.

The team will get a short reprieve when they host unranked Michigan State in the Mack Brady Match on Sept. 18, but then it’s right back on the road to face No. 22 Indiana on Sept. 25.

Last season, Penn State took a 4-1 beating from Indiana on a night that doubled as the Mack Brady Match and the alumni weekend celebration.

Just three days later, UCLA travels to Jeffrey Field. The Bruins won the 2025 Big Ten Tournament and earned the conference’s automatic bid to the NCAA Tournament.

Then comes the rivalry swing. Penn State will take on Ohio State at home before flying to Ann Arbor to battle Michigan.

The Nittany Lions took the Wolverines to a thrilling 0-0 draw in last year’s regular season finale on a soggy night at Jeffrey Field. At the time, Michigan was No. 10 in the country and touting an 11-2-3 record.

Dow’s squad will then return to the Midwest to face Northwestern on Oct. 18. The Wildcats are coming off of a season in which they tied for seventh in the Big Ten and earned an 8-6-3 overall record. That could be an opportunity to pick off an elusive road victory.

Late in the season, Penn State plays three home games in eight days against Rutgers, Wisconsin and Duquesne.

Rutgers and Wisconsin, both mediocre Big Ten programs, will serve as strong measuring sticks for the success of Dow’s first season. A pair of victories would ensure that the Nittany Lions emerged from the conference’s basement, while convincing losses would feel eerily similar to 2024 and 2025.

The blue and white will likely celebrate senior night with the home finale against Duquesne on Oct. 28. The Dukes went undefeated in non-conference play last season, but stumbled through A-10 play to a 2-6 conference record.

The regular season comes to a close with a trip to College Park to battle the defending Big Ten regular season champions. Maryland did not lose a home game last season and reached the quarterfinals of the NCAA Tournament. This year, the Terps look formidable again, sitting at No. 7 in the United Soccer Coaches Preseason Poll.

With seven opponents on the schedule that defeated the Nittany Lions last year, the Big Ten is pulling no punches. Dow’s first season in blue and white will be one to pay close attention to as Penn State men’s soccer enters its next chapter.

title: Penn State’s special teamers emphasize 'synergy,' brotherhood ahead of 2026 season
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
When the field goal unit takes the field this fall, long snapper Blaise Sokach-Minnick, punter and holder Nathan Tiyce and kicker Ryan Barker are meant to be a single entity. Throughout the offseason, the three of them have been putting in work to build trust and a routine that works for them.

Barker, Tiyce and Sokach-Minnick sat together at local media day on Friday, sharing laughs about their gameday superstitions and who's better at what video game, but also spoke about their important relationship on and off the field while they “strive for perfection.”

“The big piece of it is the synergy,” Barker said at local media day. “Being able to be on the same page pretty much all the time when we're on the field and making sure that we're kind of moving with the same intentionality as each other. That's the only way we're going to make strides day to day.”

Last season, Barker’s chemistry with long snapper Tyler Duzansky and holder Riley Thompson was crucial to his 94.7% field goal conversion rate, a single-season Penn State record.

A similar tandem appears to be on the rise as Sokach-Minnick was under direct tutelage from Duzansky, who is a rookie with the Las Vegas Raiders, and Chris Stoll, who won the Patrick Mannelly Award given annually to the nation’s best long snapper in 2022.

Tiyce, meanwhile, is Australian-born just like Thompson.

“As an Australian, it's a natural thing you do growing up,” Tiyce said. “Instead of going to throw the football with your mates down the park, you end up just going to kick the football with your mates down the park.”

The chemistry between the new tandem is already being shown at the start of fall camp. Sokach-Minnick noted that because of the sheer number of reps since January, the others know to correct mistakes quickly.

“I know that Nate's going to make me right,” Sokach-Minnick said. “And we all have the ultimate faith in Barker to ultimately get the job done. So, I think it's the trust in having each other's back that just builds confidence, our routine and leads to us executing.”

Special teams coordinator Justin Lustig has been preaching the “one shot, one kill” mantra all offseason long, meaning the trio’s focus is only on executing the play in front of them. It’s a motto that the three have embraced, fully understanding the pressures of having to make good on every individual opportunity.

Additionally, for a group of positions that don’t always jump out on the box score, the three are fully committed to the team before individual honors, despite Barker and Sokach-Minnick’s expectations from being named to the Lou Groza and Mannelly watch lists respectively.

“It's not a glamorous position whatsoever,” Tiyce said. “None of us are here for accolades or anything like that. We're here to make out what we can do for the team and improve the field position for our team or put points on the board.”

The three take their friendship off the field as well, spending a lot of time together away from the football facilities to get on the “same wavelength,” according to Tiyce. Having the same mindset during both practice and a game allows them to act on instinct and avoid falling victim to the pressure that awaits in Beaver Stadium.

“It's just like we're mates,” Tiyce said. “We just know what everyone's thinking, and it's just a nice little battery going on.”

title: How Penn State lettermen Michael Mauti, Jordan Hill are making an impact with new coaching staff
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Before Penn State left for the summer, Matt Campbell took the team to watch Saving the Roar, a documentary that detailed the adversity and hardships the 2012 program faced after the death of Joe Paterno and aftermath of the Jerry Sandusky scandal.

At the time, former Nittany Lion Jordan Hill was already on staff as director of player development and Michael Mauti served as the director of development for Penn State Athletics. Both were important members of the 2012 team, serving as veteran leaders during times of trouble.

“(The film) paid a great tribute to who Mike really was and what he stood for,” Campbell said at local media day on Friday. “When our players watched that film and understood what him, Jordan Hill, what those guys stood for, I think it was a monumental growth moment for a football team to really understand what it means to play here and have those guys around us every day means a lot.”

Nearly two months later, Mauti transitioned to a role as director of football engagement, a position Campbell advocated to give the former linebacker great with Vice President of Intercollegiate Athletics Pat Kraft.

As the team has returned to the practice field, they’ve continued to interact with Hill, who is now the director of the Nittany Lions’ Lettermen’s Club, and Mauti. The exposure to these lettermen has given Penn State’s current players a chance to learn from those who have experienced the highs and lows of playing in Happy Valley.

“I think it’s awesome to have someone that has accomplished what (Mauti) has here,” D’Anton Lynn said. “For our players to have access to him, whether it’s at breakfast or lunch. The more guys that can be around our players, I think it’s just awesome.”

Campbell has also noticed Mauti’s passion for the program, saying he was “just struck by his passion for what Penn State is about.” That sentiment has carried over to the players as well, who’ve enjoyed the opportunity to be around Mauti.

“He’s super genuine, doesn’t really care about what he’s done in the past,” linebacker Caleb Bacon said. “He cares more about what he can do for the future, how he can get around the program. He’s been awesome to talk to.”

However, Mauti is far from the only Nittany Lion leaving an impression on Penn State's current players, as Hill has also become a familiar presence around the program in his new role and while Campbell continues to emphasize the program’s rich history.

“(He’s) a heck of a player,” Lynn said. “When he was here, he was one of the hardest working guys on the team. Having someone like him, the type of person he is and player he was, to be around our players every single day, I think he’s the perfect person for it.”

title: Looking to trade ‘thingamabobs’? Newly opened Happy Valley Trinket Trade Box has you covered
author: Samantha Cormier | For the Collegian
description:
State College trinket lovers now have a place to trade stickers, pins, fidgets and other knick knacks.

The Happy Valley Trinket Trade Box, which launched on July 15, provides a place for people of all ages to trade and collect small items. The box was originally located at 100 Hiester St, East End Social, however it will soon be relocated to the Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Plaza.

Laura Collazo, a self-proclaimed trinket lover, said she pitched the idea to the Downtown State College Improvement District after noticing a lack of trinket boxes in the area. It approved the endeavor, allowing her to place the box at East End Social, a seasonal pocket park.

“If you want something done, you gotta do it yourself,” Collazo said. “That was (DSCID) first helping me out, and then they were going to help me find a permanent partner. but they ended up deciding that they would be the permanent partner.”

Collazo will soon be moving to Bellefonte, Pennsylvania, and said this is her way of leaving a bit of herself in State College.

“I wanted to put a little joy back into the community because it's given me so much,” Collazo said. “And so I said that's gonna be my resolution. I'm gonna open a trinket box before I leave, so I get to do my very first trade somewhere, and then just leave something here.”

Collazo said launching the trinket trade box took a village, and she’s consistently receiving recommendations on how to improve it from community members.

“So it really is the community that has brought this project to life,” Collazo said.

While the box stands without consistent supervision, there are guidelines in place to help maintain the safety of its visitors and items inside. No food, drinks or other perishable items are allowed and all trinkets must be family friendly, according to a post pinned on trade box’s Instagram account.

Since the box opened, Collazo has arranged three themed drops: A local artist spotlight, a food-themed trinket drop and, most recently, a Pokémon theme.

As part of the local artist tribute, Bee Slater chose to feature her own artwork in the box.

“I wanted to make a version of my sculptures that was more accessible, so I made a 2D version

of the 3D taking sculptures I’ve actually made and then illustrating them digitally into stickers and pins,” Slater, a third-year studying visual arts with a specialization in sculpture, said.

Slater is a one-man-band, painting all of her work digitally, pressing her own pins and cutting everything by hand.

“I really like putting my stickers in (the box), particularly my rat sticker,” Slater said. “Because (it’s been) awesome to be able to see people I don’t know and then see on their laptop or on their water bottle my sticker that I designed. It’s the coolest feeling.”

When Arial Monica found the box, scrolling through her TikTok feed, she said it seemed like a fun activity for her and her children to enjoy together.

“I just really love tiny things … I like the little stuff that’s put in it, and it’s fun for kids,” Monica, a digital content creator, said. “I think it’s just everybody sharing their own ideas, and opinions, just in a very subtle way.”

title: ‘I bend my social media to what I do in real life’ | Student influencers bring personal brands to campus
author: Sarah Price | For the Collegian
description:
No matter how much the internet evolves, one of its byproducts has remained consistent: The popularity of social media.

Social media started as online forums and plain profiles; as an easier way to check up on one’s friends. But today, rather than being used just to communicate, social media is also used to influence. At Penn State, many student influencers are taking advantage of this, and it’s yielding results from brand deals to modeling.

Zac Calamita, a second-year studying secondary English education, has been active on social media since middle school, but he recently found campus fame by posting food reviews on TikTok — a platform on which he has nearly 9,000 followers.

Coincidentally, Calamita’s first viral video was the first food review video he ever posted. He was in the East Food District Buffet eating pesto pasta, breadsticks and cauliflower when the idea to film a review settled in.

“The lighting was really good where I was sitting. And I was like, ‘Wait, this would be so funny if I made a whole video about this,’” Calamita said.

That video started to gain traction on TikTok, alongside a dorm tour he posted later that same day.

Last school year, Calamita became one of the first official Penn State Brand Ambassadors, alongside several other campus influencers.

“It’s a really cool program, and it’s given me a way to not only connect with the audience a little bit more, but it’s also given me amazing connections with other brand ambassadors in the program,” Calamita said.

Because he mainly focuses on food reviews, he said he finds it easy to do, because eating is a daily occurrence, not something he has to go out of his way to do.

Mkenna Gerard, a fourth-year studying advertising, is building up her platform on TikTok.

Gerard is now entering her second term as a Penn State Social Media Intern.

“I think that also allowed me to embrace more of not being as uncomfortable with filming in public or making videos with people,” Gerard said.

As a Red Bull Student Marketeer at Penn State, Gerard said it’s the “coolest opportunity” to gain hands-on experience with the brand, as well as share it on campus. Though she’s allocating a lot of time to extending her personal brand and getting to meet more people, she said school still comes first.

“I came to college to get the degree, and advertising is a major that’s so important with all of the connections you make,” Gerard said.

Sophia Mamunes, a second-year studying graphic design, had her first moment of virality when she partook in a simple TikTok trend with her senior year prom dress. Her video received millions of views in just a few days.

Ever since that post, Mamunes said being a student influencer has given her an endless amount of opportunities, both on and off campus. She now has over 28,000 followers on TikTok, and has continued to post fashion and lifestyle content.

She said she knew coming to Penn State would be a big opportunity, marketing wise.

“I find that if you just say what you feel on the internet, usually other kids your age are also feeling that same way,” Mamunes said.

Mamunes said it’s easy for her to balance her content and academics. It doesn’t take much time to set up her phone and film a quick video before heading to class, she said.

“I don’t really like to cater my life to social media. I bend my social media to what I do in real life,” Mamunes said.

Just last week, Mamunes entered the world of modeling, and — in a full circle moment — did a runway show with the brand AMARRA, the company that designed the prom dress from her first viral video.

She said it’s been “really cool” to connect with women across the country who have similar interests and aspirations.

“Understand that there may be negative comments at times,” Mamunes said. “But continuing to post is always worth it, because of the opportunities you might get in the long run.”

title: Penn State WR Peter Gonzalez ready ‘to do whatever I can to help the team’ in return from injury
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Wide receiver Peter Gonzalez came to Penn State in 2024 as a 3-star recruit with a big frame, hoping to be part of a receiver surge that the Nittany Lions desperately needed at the time.

But things didn’t quite go to plan for Gonzalez, now a redshirt sophomore, who has recently just fully recovered from a second consecutive season-ending injury.

“I just want to do whatever I can to help the team, whatever that role looks like,” Gonzalez said. “I'm just excited to get out there and do what I have to do.”

Gonzalez dealt with two long seasons, both of which he had to watch a majority from the sideline as he dealt with major injuries. Regardless, the perseverance from the Pennsylvania native has allowed him to grow off the field.

That off-field mentality has earned recognition from his peers and position coaches. It’s tough to stay mentally strong while not being able to participate at all on the field during the week or on Saturdays.

“You talk about a young man that has dealt with adversity, right?” wide receivers coach Kashif Moore said at local media day. “But has shown so much perseverance, because of going through those things, man, it's made him stronger mentally. He has a way of always being optimistic, always being positive.”

Gonzalez pointed to one person who helped him stay mentally strong during those two years — His dad, former NFL quarterback Pete Gonzalez, was his mentor and go-to person during that time, calling him his “biggest influence throughout this whole journey.”

“He's been the reason I've been able to keep my head down, keep my head on straight, and continue grinding despite what things look like,” Gonzalez said. “He has a very interesting story of his career, and I can take pride in knowing that he kept his head down, he kept working, and that led to him getting what he wanted and more. So he's been my biggest inspiration. He's my hero, and I'm really just trying to emulate what he did and make it my own and make them proud.”

Gonzalez has put himself in position to be in the conversation in a growingly crowded receiver room due to working “really closely with the new staff and the new trainers” and getting his “body back to an amazing position.”

The depth, which includes Gonzalez, in addition to top-end talent has the room confident that major success under Taylor Mouser’s system is coming.

That confidence extends to the players themselves, especially Gonzalez, who has shown out in practices. With him getting back into form, Gonzalez could see playing time in Beaver Stadium for the first time in his career.

“I mean that's something I've been waiting for, for two years-plus when I was a recruit,” Gonzalez said. “Just being able to suit up and be on that field as a player is something that I've dreamed about and that I've seen for the last two years and just been yearning for. So to get in front of that crowd, get in front of those people, and hope to make some plays that would be amazing.”

title: ‘Sponge to information’ | Penn State S Jamison Patton taking advantage of first-team reps
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Jamison Patton has lined up across from Marcus Neal Jr. at fall camp for first-team safety reps while a recovering Jeremiah Cooper has worked off to the side, now in the late stages of rehabbing his September ACL tear.

A starter last year at Iowa State, Patton’s junior season was cut short after nine games due to a lower-body injury. During his time away from the gridiron, he made significant strides improving his physique.

“This particular offseason, he's probably made the biggest change to his body,” safeties coach Deon Broomfield said at local media day on Friday. “From body fat percentage, he's leaner, he's hitting speeds that he's never hit before.”

The physical change wasn’t the only thing that stuck out to Broomfield. Patton has grown to be more confident and is a leader on the field, forming a reputation among his teammates as someone who always knows what to do.

A former quarterback for three years in high school, Patton has brought his comfortability in leadership roles to the college setting. While he’s not slinging the ball around or commanding the offense anymore, he’s no stranger to getting up in front of his teammates and being vocal, an aspect Broomfield dubbed Patton’s “special sauce.”

“Whatever I see, I'm communicating that and letting people know,” Patton said. “But it's just being on the same page. Nothing in football is going to be perfect. You may miss some tackles, but one thing we can control is communication and having everybody on the same page to succeed.”

It’s these traits that actively coincide with D’Anton Lynn’s “obnoxious communication” and Broomfield’s “keep no secrets” mantras. Broomfield noticed these alignments and is now letting Patton show it on the field.

But for Patton, getting first-team reps again isn't about potentially replacing Cooper as the team’s starter. It reflects the depth of the safety room, backed by the genuine desire to experience collective growth, with Patton calling the current situation a “friendly competition.”

“Coming from Iowa State, we preach ‘Mudita,’ which is authentic joy for other’s success,” Patton said. “That's how we're wired, how we've ingrained in our mind that authentic joy for seeing our brothers succeed. We're all trying to do what's best for the team, and with that mindset, you can't really have any problems.”

Patton downplayed the first-team reps, as the depth chart is never truly set, something Matt Campbell emphasized on Friday as well. Instead, Patton is focused on the “things that take no talent.”

These, Patton noted, are high-level communication, effort, being a “sponge to information” and working to put his teammates in positions to succeed.

While Cooper remains Penn State’s projected starting free safety, the room has another waiting in the wings when needed.

“(Patton is) very smart, very versatile, just a great player to play across,” Cooper said. “I’ve played more years than him, but I'm still learning things from him and from Marcus. Making each other better every single day, I feel like that's the biggest strength to our room, along with the connection we have together.”

title: Former Penn State OT Caedan Wallace traded to Miami Dolphins by New England Patriots
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
A former Penn Stater will have to find a new home.

Offensive tackle Caedan Wallace was traded by the New England Patriots to the Miami Dolphins on Monday, per Jordan Schultz. The Patriots are sending Wallace and a 2029 seventh-round pick in exchange for a 2028 sixth-round pick.

The Patriots initially planned to release Wallace, but the Dolphins came in and scooped him up before he became a free agent.

Wallace, who was drafted by New England in the third-round of the 2024 NFL Draft, appeared in six games as a rookie, starting in two of them. That October, he was placed on injured reserve.

The following year, the former Nittany Lion appeared in four more games, but did not play in the postseason during the Patriots run to the Super Bowl.

With Penn State, Wallace started in 40 games across five years. In his redshirt senior season, he allowed just one sack in 359 pass blocking snaps.

title: Penn State onboards 2 AI-specialized, tenure-track music professors
author: Saxtyn Lutz | The Daily Collegian
description:
The College of Arts and Architecture's School of Music has recruited two tenure-track faculty members who specialize in the intersection of music and artificial intelligence (AI).

Last year, the Institute for Computational and Data Sciences began a multi-year cluster hire integrating AI into academic research across all disciplines. In April, students protested outside of the music buildings in opposition of the School of Music’s search for such hires. Their signs read, “My tuition won’t fund AI slop,” “Support artists not algorithms” and “We will not be replaced by AI.”

Colin Stokes and Jacob Holster are the new co-hires with the ICDS and the School of Music. Stokes will serve as an assistant professor of music and AI and Holster an assistant professor of music education and AI, both starting this fall.

“(The role) hasn't been fully defined yet, which is so exciting,” Stokes said. “I have the freedom to pursue my work as a composer, as a cellist, as a researcher and as an educator, so it's artistically just a very good fit.”

Stokes said his understanding of human involvement in AI is based on the philosophy of Luciano Floridi, who argued technology is not inherently neutral and is subject to forces that push it into what society perceives as morally good or morally evil directions.

The announcement of his new position on social media was met with backlash, to which he said he is glad students are using their voices. He added that he hopes students can have conversations with him about his work and research.

“I can let people know about the actual work I'm doing, which is not so big and scary,” Stokes said. “It’s ... little tools that I find to be useful for me and my colleagues.”

Stokes will teach a section of Music 40, the first-year seminar course for music students. He said the class is focused on getting to know the university and developing skills to be a successful college student.

AI will not be used in any of the course materials or for grading, he said, and does not intend to make AI use mandatory in the classroom. He also said he will not use AI to grade assignments.

Holster, previously on the non-tenure track, will begin his sixth year at Penn State in the fall.

His current research revolves around music and teacher education. Using AI, he develops tools for future educators to practice teaching. On ChatGPT, a widely used LLM, he’s developed a tool called Classroom Coach, which creates fictitious scenarios teachers may encounter with students. The user can interact with the system to practice responding to situations.

Presently, within music education research, academics are discussing when AI should and should not be used based on their understanding of the risks and philosophical questions it poses, Holster said.

“I think folks should be able to question what AIs they use, what they refuse to use and look at the refusal as an informed process of actually understanding AI more,” Holster said. “I hope folks will be, at the very least, more open to conversation about it.”

Holster will be teaching the general education course, AA 290G: Creating and Learning with AI, he co-created within the College of Arts and Architecture. The course has been offered since the Spring 2025 semester. He will also be helping graduate students in the Ph.D. music education program develop research agendas.

Holster said his current philosophy is an openness to what the profession needs and allowing students to shape their future field. He said no one will be forced to use AI, and no one is going to be asked to discuss AI if they don’t feel comfortable with the conversation.

“Music teaching and learning has always been a very slow, changing process,” Holster said. “It's arts-based and experience-based, and if a technology takes away from that experience, folks are gonna reject it.”

Ann Marie Stanley, director of the School of Music, said there have been large conversations at the collegiate level about the need to address ethical, environmental, industry and cultural aspects of AI. She said all of these issues are elemental to the role and responsibility of the College of Arts and Architecture, as artists, designers and educators.

“I want to assure everyone that we will not be replacing human creativity, musicianship or compositional craft with generative AI in our program at Penn State,” Stanley said. “I'm grateful for (student) input, their conversation and any conversations we'll have in the future, because it is a thorny issue.”

Various universities, such as Ohio State, University of Florida, University of Wisconsin-Madison and Northwestern have recently brought in music and AI professors, according to Stanley.

She said it’s important Penn State found skilled musician researchers to ask the hardest questions about what AI means for music, and give them resources to find answers and teach about it.

“I want a strong voice with these outstanding teachers and researchers,” Stanley said. “I want a strong voice from Penn State School of Music part of that conversation.”

title: ‘I really believe in these guys’ | 3 things we heard about Penn State’s OL at local media day
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Ryan Clanton followed Matt Campbell to Penn State and has established an offensive line with returners and transfers alike.

As the season draws near, the staff and players have seen development and growth from the line as they continue to work through fall camp.

Here’s what Campbell, Clanton and other players and coaches said about the offensive line’s success this offseason at local media day on Friday.

Anthony Donkoh's return

An unspecified medical procedure sidelined Anthony Donkoh for spring practice, limiting what Penn State’s new coaching staff could see from its most experienced tackle. Despite being the biggest returner for the Nittany Lions, Campbell and Clanton hadn’t seen what he was capable of.

Donkoh returned to practice in early August and immediately became a focal point in the offense. He was deemed a leader by the coaching staff and players and was one of Penn State’s representatives at Big Ten Media Days in Chicago.

“I think it’s a calming factor for me when you have a guy like that that has the experience and the skill set that he has,” Taylor Mouser said. “You want a guy that’s one of the best leaders on offense to be one of your tackles.”

While Donkoh played under Phil Trautwein for his first three seasons, he’s been quick to learn the new system under Clanton and help the younger players adapt as well, saying “that’s my role, trying to be able to give back and raise everybody up and get them up to speed.”

“They understand that we teach that the way they have been taught in the past isn’t wrong, it’s just different,” Clanton said. “So they have a good understanding of how we want to do things and break old habits. They really want to do what’s best for the team.”

Chemistry up front

While Penn State returns some veterans Donkoh, Dom Rulli and Cooper Cousins, it also retained young talents Malachi Goodman, Garrett Sexton and Owen Aliciene while bringing in transfers Brock Riker and Trevor Buhr.

Amidst the many new faces and depth chart uncertainty, the 20 offensive linemen on Penn State’s roster have created a sense of brotherhood and chemistry well before the season has started.

“I feel like O-linemen are pretty easy to like. I get along with everyone in the room and people get along with me,” Sexton said. “I feel like we’ve been meshing really well.”

While a majority of the linemen are either returners to Happy Valley or came over from Iowa State, Riker transferred from Texas State and has worked to fit in with the other pre-established groups on the team.

“Everyone was new to me, but they welcomed me with open arms,” Riker said. “They helped me, whether that be with the playbook or where to go. They were very supportive of me.”

On the field, the players have had to adjust to Clanton’s game plan and style of culture as well.

Clanton sat his squad down on the first day of fall camp and went through the rules and regulations he has for the program, including necessities for various positions and his expectations for the program.

“If you can be violent and you can try to run through somebody's face, that's requirement one for us,” Clanton said.

Depth chart battles

Since Goodman arrived at Penn State as a 4-star recruit, there’s been a lot of praise for his talents and excitement for his potential. This offseason, the coaching staff has seen that play out, as Campbell called Goodman “one of the best humans that I have met since I’ve been here.”

At the same time, however, Campbell addressed the current weaknesses in Goodman’s game that are allowing Sexton and Aliciene to stay alive in the battle for left tackle.

“Malachi has elite traits in every way, shape and form,” Campbell said. “Anytime you have a young player that’s got elite traits, what you’re looking for is can you consistently do your job? Can you consistently be counted on?”

Also in a position battle are centers Riker and Rulli. Throughout summer workouts and the first two days of fall camp, Clanton continued to swap pieces of his offensive line in and out as he worked to find the best starting five.

“You can put a mixture of any five guys out there and you’re going to get a consistent product,” Clanton said. “The depth that we have makes us special and I really believe in these guys and what they’re about.”

As his squad has continued to play with different lineups, he’s praised their ability to continue to get more reps, even if a player is working with first team one day and third team another.

Clanton compared his team’s success and determination with that of his former prodigy at Northern Iowa, Spencer Brown, who is now a left tackle with the Buffalo Bills. During a practice, Clanton said Brown worked with the backups and how it was “one of the most violent practices he’d ever seen.”

“There’s not really even a switch between shutting down or fighting harder, they’re just consistent,” Clanton said. “We’ve got ways of motivating them, but those guys have done a great job of just consistently attacking.”

title: 3 Penn State women’s volleyball players that could break out in 2026
author: Rafael Rivera | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State women’s volleyball’s 2026 campaign is looming, with the season starting Aug. 27 at the inaugural Spikes Under The Lights Tournament.

The team has many players that could potentially break out and have a stellar season. Here are three of them.

Emmi Sellman, outside hitter

The Burtonsville, Maryland Native was the No. 5 overall prospect in the 2024 class and a two-time Gatorade Player of the Year at the Academy of the Holy Cross.

Sellman played her Freshman season at Ohio State, totaling 219 kills and 128 digs earning Big Ten All-Freshman Team honors before transferring to Penn State in December of 2024.

In Sellman's 2025 season, she tallied 257 kills, 41 blocks and 10 aces. Sellman is poised to have a breakout 2026 because she’ll be stepping into a primary left-side attacker role left open by All-American star Jess Mruzik.

Sellman has proven that she can compete against elite teams, racking up 16 kills with a highly efficient 12 digs against No.14 Kansas. In 2024 when she played for Ohio State, she put on a 27-kill performance against the Nittany Lions.

All American teammate Kennedy Martin will command lots of attention from opposing teams, leaving middle blockers to cheat towards her and form double blocks, leaving Sellman isolated on the left. The 6-foot-4 outside hitter can be a true weapon for Nittany Lions in her Junior season.

Alexis Ewing, outside hitter

The six-foot-four daughter of NBA hall-of-famer Patrick Ewing and volleyball star Cheryl Weaver hails from Bethesda, Maryland, where she attended the Bullis School.

In high school, Ewing was a 2024 AVCA Second-Team All-American and the Washington Post All-Met Player of the year. In her Freshman year with the Nittany Lions, she totaled 77 kills and 19 blocks in 20 matches, appearing in a high stakes NCAA tournament match against Texas.

She has exceptional length and athleticism, being recognized for her elite vertical jumping ability by being named to the “10-Foot Club”after recording a 10 '4 block touch.

Ewing appeared to adjust to the speed of college volleyball and gain valuable experience. Her role is expected to expand dramatically in her sophomore season, having the same advantage as Sellman, being able to benefit off of the opposing team focusing on Kennedy Martin.

Ava Falduto, libero

The five-foot-seven junior from Elmhurst Illinois is moving into a new role in 2026. Falduto was a defensive specialist in her first two seasons in state college logging 538 total digs and 67 service aces playing in all 32 matches making 14 starts in 2025.

2026 is projected to be Falduto's first full year as Penn State's starting libero, giving her unlimited backcourt freedom opposed to being restricted by situational substitutions.

Falduto proved herself on a national championship team in 2024, finishing with 310 digs and leading the team with 39 aces. Now, with Falduto being the leader of the backcourt, she has potential to be one of Penn State's best.

title: 5 Players to watch heading into Penn State women's soccer's 2026 season
author: Rafael Rivera | For the Collegian
description:
Penn State women's soccer’s 2026 campaign is rapidly approaching, with the blue and white opening their season on Aug. 16 against the Notre Dame Fighting Irish.

2025 was a lackluster season for women's soccer, with the team going 10-8-3 losing early in the NCAA tournament against Virginia. It was a season coming off of a year where the team had a record of 15-7-3 and went deep into the NCAA Tournament, ultimately reaching the quarterfinal.

Penn State is looking to have a bounce back year heading into the 2026 season. Here are 5 players that could lead the charge and make a difference.

Mackenzie Gress, Goalkeeper

Redshirt senior Mackenzie Gress, a 5-foot-9 goalkeeper from Lynhurst, New Jersey, will be heading into her final season as the Nittany Lions' captain. She's been Penn State's premier keeper and leader since her redshirt sophomore season where she came into her own, starring in 13 matches for the blue and white.

Gress has tallied 38 total appearances in goal, with 113 saves and seven clean cheats. In 2024, she brought home bronze for the United States U-20 Women's national team. In a 2025 match against UCLA, Gress recorded a career high nine saves, earning her a spot on the Big Ten All-Tournament team. Gress will serve as an accomplished leading veteran presence for the team in 2026.

Bella Ayscue, Defender

Bella Ayscue, a dynamic backline defender from Apex, North Carolina, has impressed in her first two seasons in State College with three goals, six assists and 19 shots on target in 46 matches played.

In 2024, Ayscue had a productive freshman campaign tallying one goal and five assists while starting in 11 of 25 of her matches played, showing that she had lots of potential to be a playmaker while also defending.

Ayscue saw the field plenty in her sophomore season, starting in all 21 games in 2025. She finished the season with the second-most minutes played at 1,819, pushing her to be nominated to the United Soccer Coaches All-North Region Third Team and the All-Big Ten third team.

She'll serve as a lockdown defender who can slow down a team's best attacking player while also being able to run up the pitch and create a scoring chance making her skillset very valuable. 2026 could be a season where Ayscue makes the jump from being good to elite.

Molly Martin, Midfield

Molly Martin, a five-foot-nine redshirt senior from Hanson, Massachusetts, is Penn State's leader in the middle.
